The ferry to the island leaves the harbor at seven every morning unless the wind is too strong for the small boat to cross safely
On calm days the crossing takes about forty minutes and the passengers sit on the upper deck to watch the gulls follow the wake
Most of the passengers are workers who keep the weather station running and a few are visitors who want to see the old lighthouse
The weather station on the island records the temperature and the wind speed every ten minutes and sends the readings to the mainland
Each reading is written to a small log file and the log file is copied to a server in the harbor office once an hour
When the radio link fails the station keeps the readings in memory and sends them all at once when the link comes back
The keeper of the station checks the instruments every morning and writes a short note about anything that looks wrong or broken
Last winter a storm bent the wind vane so badly that the station reported the same wind direction for nine days in a row
Nobody noticed the problem until a fisherman asked why the forecast said the wind came from the north when it clearly came from the west
After that the keeper wrote a small program that compares each reading with the readings from the two nearest stations on the coast
If a reading differs too much from its neighbors the program marks it as suspect and sends a message to the keeper
The program is simple and it uses a moving average of the last twelve readings to decide what counts as too much
Simple rules like this one catch most broken instruments but they also raise false alarms when a sudden squall passes over the island
To reduce the false alarms the keeper started to count how often each kind of alarm turned out to be real
Over a few months the counts showed that alarms about wind direction were usually real and alarms about temperature were usually noise
The keeper then changed the program so that temperature alarms need three suspect readings in a row before a message is sent
The ferry company also uses the readings from the station to decide whether the morning crossing should go ahead
When the wind speed at the station is above a fixed limit the company cancels the crossing and posts a notice at the harbor
Passengers who miss the morning crossing can usually take the afternoon boat because the wind tends to drop after midday
The afternoon boat is slower than the morning boat but it has a covered cabin and a small kitchen that sells tea and bread
On the island there is one shop one school and a small library that opens on tuesday and saturday afternoons
The library keeps a shelf of old station logs written by hand in thick paper notebooks before the instruments were automated
Students from the school sometimes copy numbers from the old notebooks into a spreadsheet to compare old winters with recent ones
Their spreadsheet shows that the island has fewer days of frost now than it had fifty years ago
It also shows that the strongest storms now arrive a few weeks later in the autumn than they did in the old notebooks
The teacher uses the spreadsheet to explain averages and ranges and why a single cold week says little about the climate
Some students find the old handwriting hard to read and they argue about whether a mark on the page is a seven or a one
When they cannot agree they leave the cell empty and write a comment that explains why the value is missing
The keeper likes this habit because an honest gap in the data is better than a guess that looks like a real number
Every spring the keeper and the students walk around the island and check the rain gauges that sit in the fields
The rain gauges are plain metal cylinders and the most common fault is a bird nest blocking the funnel at the top
A blocked gauge reports no rain at all which is easy to spot when every other gauge on the island reports a wet day
The students write down the state of each gauge in a notebook and the keeper later types the notes into the station log
On the walk the students also count the sheep in each field because the farmer pays them a little for an accurate count
The sheep count and the rain records are kept in separate files but the keeper once found that wet springs mean more lambs
Nobody is sure whether that pattern is real or a coincidence because there are only a dozen years of sheep counts
The keeper says that a pattern found in a dozen points should be treated as a question and not as an answer
In the summer the island fills with visitors who come on the morning ferry and leave on the last boat in the evening
Many visitors climb the hill to the old lighthouse and take pictures of the weather station from the gallery at the top
The lighthouse has not been used for many years because a small automatic beacon on the rocks now does the same job
The beacon flashes twice every ten seconds and its pattern is printed on the charts that the ferry crew use at night
The ferry crew rarely sail at night but they keep the charts up to date in case of an emergency on the island
Once a year a doctor comes over on the ferry and spends a week seeing patients in a room at the back of the school
During that week the morning crossing is always full and the ferry company sometimes adds a second boat to carry everyone
The second boat is an old fishing vessel with a loud engine and a captain who tells long stories about past storms
His favorite story is about the winter the harbor froze and the island had no ferry for almost three weeks
The weather station has no record of that winter because it was built many years later but the old notebooks mention it
According to the notebooks the keeper at the time measured the ice every day by cutting a hole and dropping a weighted line
The students like this story because it shows that careful measurement is possible even without any modern instruments
At the end of each year the keeper writes a short report that lists every fault the station had and how it was fixed
The report goes to the mainland office and a copy is placed on the library shelf next to the old notebooks
